claim: KATP channels are metabolic sensors that couple cell energetics to membrane excitability.
source: KATP channels are metabolic sensors that couple cell energetics to membrane excitability.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about KATP channel function.

claim: In pancreatic β-cells, channels formed by SUR1 and Kir6.2 regulate insulin secretion.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, channels formed by SUR1 and Kir6.2 regulate insulin secretion and are the targets of antidiabetic sulfonylureas.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KATP channel composition and function in β-cells.

claim: KATP channels formed by SUR1 and Kir6.2 are the targets of antidiabetic sulfonylureas.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, channels formed by SUR1 and Kir6.2 regulate insulin secretion and are the targets of antidiabetic sulfonylureas.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sulfonylurea drug targets.

claim: The cryo-EM structure was determined in the presence of ATP and the sulfonylurea glibenclamide at ~6 Å resolution.
source: The structure, determined in the presence of ATP and the sulfonylurea glibenclamide, at ~6 Å resolution reveals a closed Kir6.2 tetrameric core with four peripheral SUR1s each anchored to a Kir6.2 by its N-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD0).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions and resolution of the structure determination.

claim: The structure reveals a closed Kir6.2 tetrameric core with four peripheral SUR1s.
source: The structure, determined in the presence of ATP and the sulfonylurea glibenclamide, at ~6 Å resolution reveals a closed Kir6.2 tetrameric core with four peripheral SUR1s each anchored to a Kir6.2 by its N-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD0).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Each SUR1 is anchored to a Kir6.2 by its N-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD0).
source: The structure, determined in the presence of ATP and the sulfonylurea glibenclamide, at ~6 Å resolution reveals a closed Kir6.2 tetrameric core with four peripheral SUR1s each anchored to a Kir6.2 by its N-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD0).
evidence: This describes the structural interaction observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: Intricate interactions exist between TMD0, the loop following TMD0, and Kir6.2 near the proposed PIP2 binding site.
source: Intricate interactions between TMD0, the loop following TMD0, and Kir6.2 near the proposed PIP2 binding site, and where ATP density is observed, suggest SUR1 may contribute to ATP and PIP2 binding to enhance Kir6.2 sensitivity to both.
evidence: This describes structural observations from the cryo-EM map.

claim: ATP density is observed near the proposed PIP2 binding site.
source: Intricate interactions between TMD0, the loop following TMD0, and Kir6.2 near the proposed PIP2 binding site, and where ATP density is observed, suggest SUR1 may contribute to ATP and PIP2 binding to enhance Kir6.2 sensitivity to both.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: SUR1 may contribute to ATP and PIP2 binding to enhance Kir6.2 sensitivity to both.
source: Intricate interactions between TMD0, the loop following TMD0, and Kir6.2 near the proposed PIP2 binding site, and where ATP density is observed, suggest SUR1 may contribute to ATP and PIP2 binding to enhance Kir6.2 sensitivity to both.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and known functional data.

claim: The SUR1-ABC core is found in an unusual inward-facing conformation whereby the two nucleotide binding domains are misaligned along a two-fold symmetry axis.
source: The SUR1-ABC core is found in an unusual inward-facing conformation whereby the two nucleotide binding domains are misaligned along a two-fold symmetry axis, revealing a possible mechanism by which glibenclamide inhibits channel activity.
evidence: This describes a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The misalignment of NBDs reveals a possible mechanism by which glibenclamide inhibits channel activity.
source: The SUR1-ABC core is found in an unusual inward-facing conformation whereby the two nucleotide binding domains are misaligned along a two-fold symmetry axis, revealing a possible mechanism by which glibenclamide inhibits channel activity.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the structural observation.

claim: The discovery of ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels occurred in the early 1980s.
source: Studies into the electric mechanisms of insulin release of the pancreatic β-cell in the early 1980s led to the discovery and identification of an ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel as the key molecular link between glucose metabolism and insulin secretion (Ashcroft and Rorsman, 1990; Cook and Bryan, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: KATP channels are the key molecular link between glucose metabolism and insulin secretion.
source: Studies into the electric mechanisms of insulin release of the pancreatic β-cell in the early 1980s led to the discovery and identification of an ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel as the key molecular link between glucose metabolism and insulin secretion (Ashcroft and Rorsman, 1990; Cook and Bryan, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The β-cell KATP channel is a complex of two proteins: Kir6.2 and SUR1.
source: Subsequent cloning and characterization revealed the β-cell KATP channel as a complex of two proteins: a potassium channel Kir6.2 of the inwardly rectifying K+ channel family, and a sulfonylurea receptor SUR1, a member of the ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein family (Inagaki et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Kir6.2 is a potassium channel of the inwardly rectifying K+ channel family.
source: Subsequent cloning and characterization revealed the β-cell KATP channel as a complex of two proteins: a potassium channel Kir6.2 of the inwardly rectifying K+ channel family, and a sulfonylurea receptor SUR1, a member of the ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein family (Inagaki et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SUR1 is a member of the ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein family.
source: Subsequent cloning and characterization revealed the β-cell KATP channel as a complex of two proteins: a potassium channel Kir6.2 of the inwardly rectifying K+ channel family, and a sulfonylurea receptor SUR1, a member of the ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein family (Inagaki et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ATP inhibits KATP channel activity.
source: Physiological activity of KATP channels is determined primarily by the relative concentrations of ATP and ADP: ATP inhibits, whereas MgADP stimulates channel activity (Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MgADP stimulates KATP channel activity.
source: Physiological activity of KATP channels is determined primarily by the relative concentrations of ATP and ADP: ATP inhibits, whereas MgADP stimulates channel activity (Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: KATP channels set the β-cell membrane potential.
source: As KATP channels set the β-cell membrane potential, this regulation by nucleotides endows them the ability to sense metabolic changes and translate those into changes in membrane excitability, which ultimately initiates or stops insulin secretion (Ashcroft, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Regulation of KATP channels by nucleotides allows them to sense metabolic changes and translate those into changes in membrane excitability.
source: As KATP channels set the β-cell membrane potential, this regulation by nucleotides endows them the ability to sense metabolic changes and translate those into changes in membrane excitability, which ultimately initiates or stops insulin secretion (Ashcroft, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Changes in KATP channel activity ultimately initiate or stop insulin secretion.
source: As KATP channels set the β-cell membrane potential, this regulation by nucleotides endows them the ability to sense metabolic changes and translate those into changes in membrane excitability, which ultimately initiates or stops insulin secretion (Ashcroft, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PIP2 is required for KATP channel opening.
source: Another key player for KATP function is membrane phosphatidylinositol-4, 5-bisphosphate (PIP2); as in all other Kir family members, PIP2 is required for channel opening and sets the intrinsic open probability (Po) of the channel (Hibino et al., 2010; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PIP2 sets the intrinsic open probability (Po) of KATP channels.
source: Another key player for KATP function is membrane phosphatidylinositol-4, 5-bisphosphate (PIP2); as in all other Kir family members, PIP2 is required for channel opening and sets the intrinsic open probability (Po) of the channel (Hibino et al., 2010; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in KATP channels cause congenital hyperinsulinism (HI).
source: Mutations disrupting channel assembly or the above-gating properties result in insulin secretion disorders, with loss- or gain-of-function mutations causing congenital hyperinsulinism (HI) or permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (PNDM), respectively (Ashcroft, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in KATP channels cause permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (PNDM).
source: Mutations disrupting channel assembly or the above-gating properties result in insulin secretion disorders, with loss- or gain-of-function mutations causing congenital hyperinsulinism (HI) or permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (PNDM), respectively (Ashcroft, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Sulfonylureas are one of the most commonly prescribed treatments for type 2 diabetes.
source: Importantly, KATP channels are the targets of sulfonylureas, one of the most commonly prescribed treatments for type 2 diabetes, which stimulate insulin secretion by inhibiting channel activity (Gribble and Reimann, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion by inhibiting KATP channel activity.
source: Importantly, KATP channels are the targets of sulfonylureas, one of the most commonly prescribed treatments for type 2 diabetes, which stimulate insulin secretion by inhibiting channel activity (Gribble and Reimann, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Glibenclamide binds KATP channels with nanomolar affinity.
source: In particular, glibenclamide (GBC) binds the channel with nanomolar affinity and was instrumental for the purification and cloning of SUR1 (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Glibenclamide was instrumental for the purification and cloning of SUR1.
source: In particular, glibenclamide (GBC) binds the channel with nanomolar affinity and was instrumental for the purification and cloning of SUR1 (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Kir6.2 consists of two transmembrane helices and N- and C-terminal cytoplasmic domains.
source: A member of the Kir channel family, Kir6.2 consists of two transmembrane helices and N- and C-terminal cytoplasmic domains (Hibino et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SUR1 has an N-terminal extension containing a transmembrane domain (TMD0) followed by a long cytoplasmic loop 'L0'.
source: In addition to a characteristic ABC core structure comprising two transmembrane domains (TMD1 and 2) and two cytoplasmic nucleotide binding domains (NBD1 and 2), it has an N-terminal extension that contains a transmembrane domain (TMD0) followed by a long, cytoplasmic loop 'L0' which connects to the ABC core (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Tusnády et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Kir6.2 and SUR1 are uniquely dependent on each other for expression and function.
source: Kir6.2 and SUR1 are uniquely dependent on each other for expression and function (Inagaki et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SUR1 itself has no known ion channel or transporter activity.
source: Interestingly, unlike most ABC transporters such as the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) and the multidrug-resistant protein P-glycoprotein, SUR1 itself has no known ion channel or transporter activity; instead, its function is to regulate Kir6.2 channels (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Inagaki et al., 1995; Wilkens, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The function of SUR1 is to regulate Kir6.2 channels.
source: Interestingly, unlike most ABC transporters such as the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) and the multidrug-resistant protein P-glycoprotein, SUR1 itself has no known ion channel or transporter activity; instead, its function is to regulate Kir6.2 channels (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Inagaki et al., 1995; Wilkens, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The KATP channel is an octamer of four Kir6.2 and four SUR1 subunits.
source: Biochemical and biophysical studies have indicated that the KATP channel is an octamer of four Kir6.2 and four SUR1 subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: ATP and PIP2 bind Kir6.2 directly to close or open the channel, respectively.
source: ATP and PIP2 bind Kir6.2 directly to close or open the channel, respectively (Baukrowitz et al., 1998; Shyng and Nichols, 1998; Tanabe et al., 1999; Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Kir6.2 alone can be gated by ATP and PIP2.
source: Although Kir6.2 alone can be gated by ATP and PIP2, its sensitivities to both ATP and PIP2 are increased by SUR1 by ~10-fold (Baukrowitz et al., 1998; Enkvetchakul et al., 2000; Shyng and Nichols, 1998; Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SUR1 increases Kir6.2 sensitivities to both ATP and PIP2 by ~10-fold.
source: Although Kir6.2 alone can be gated by ATP and PIP2, its sensitivities to both ATP and PIP2 are increased by SUR1 by ~10-fold (Baukrowitz et al., 1998; Enkvetchakul et al., 2000; Shyng and Nichols, 1998; Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ATP inhibition of KATP channels does not depend on Mg2+ and ATP hydrolysis.
source: In contrast to ATP inhibition of the channel, which does not depend on Mg2+ and ATP hydrolysis, nucleotide stimulation of the channel is conferred by SUR1 and requires Mg2+ (Ashcroft and Gribble, 1998; Gribble et al., 1997, 1998; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nucleotide stimulation of KATP channels is conferred by SUR1 and requires Mg2+.
source: In contrast to ATP inhibition of the channel, which does not depend on Mg2+ and ATP hydrolysis, nucleotide stimulation of the channel is conferred by SUR1 and requires Mg2+ (Ashcroft and Gribble, 1998; Gribble et al., 1997, 1998; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MgATP and MgADP interact with the nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) of SUR1.
source: Evidence suggests that MgATP and MgADP interact with the nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) of SUR1 and either through MgATP hydrolysis or through direct MgADP binding at NBD2, promote NBDs dimerization and channel opening (de Wet et al., 2012; Nichols, 2006; Zingman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MgATP hydrolysis or direct MgADP binding at NBD2 promotes NBDs dimerization and channel opening.
source: Evidence suggests that MgATP and MgADP interact with the nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) of SUR1 and either through MgATP hydrolysis or through direct MgADP binding at NBD2, promote NBDs dimerization and channel opening (de Wet et al., 2012; Nichols, 2006; Zingman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GBC has been proposed to inhibit KATP channels by preventing Mg-nucleotide stimulation.
source: Moreover, GBC has been proposed to inhibit KATP channels by preventing Mg-nucleotide stimulation (de Wet and Proks, 2015), and may do so by stabilizing the ABC core of SUR1 in an inward-facing conformation (Ortiz et al., 2012) but direct evidence is lacking.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: GBC may inhibit KATP channels by stabilizing the ABC core of SUR1 in an inward-facing conformation.
source: Moreover, GBC has been proposed to inhibit KATP channels by preventing Mg-nucleotide stimulation (de Wet and Proks, 2015), and may do so by stabilizing the ABC core of SUR1 in an inward-facing conformation (Ortiz et al., 2012) but direct evidence is lacking.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous studies supported by citations, but the text notes direct evidence is lacking.

claim: Rat insulinoma INS-1 cells naturally express KATP channels.
source: To obtain sufficient quantity of purified channel complexes, we used rat insulinoma INS-1 cells, which naturally express KATP channels, for overexpression.
evidence: This is a statement about the cell line used in the study.

claim: Cells were transduced with recombinant adenoviruses encoding genes for a FLAG-tagged hamster SUR1 and a rat Kir6.2.
source: Cells were transduced with recombinant adenoviruses encoding genes for a FLAG-tagged hamster SUR1 and a rat Kir6.2 (Pratt et al., 2009), which are 95% and 96% identical to the human sequences, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Hamster SUR1 is 95% identical to the human sequence.
source: Cells were transduced with recombinant adenoviruses encoding genes for a FLAG-tagged hamster SUR1 and a rat Kir6.2 (Pratt et al., 2009), which are 95% and 96% identical to the human sequences, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement of sequence identity.

claim: Rat Kir6.2 is 96% identical to the human sequence.
source: Cells were transduced with recombinant adenoviruses encoding genes for a FLAG-tagged hamster SUR1 and a rat Kir6.2 (Pratt et al., 2009), which are 95% and 96% identical to the human sequences, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement of sequence identity.

claim: Heterologously expressed channels have gating properties indistinguishable from endogenous KATP channels.
source: These heterologously expressed channels have gating properties indistinguishable from endogenous KATP channels (Pratt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Channel integrity was best preserved when membranes were solubilized in digitonin and channels purified in the presence of 1 µM glibenclamide (GBC) and 1 mM ATP.
source: Channel integrity was found to be best preserved when membranes were solubilized in digitonin and channels purified in the presence of 1 µM glibenclamide (GBC) and 1 mM ATP (see Materials and methods) (Figure 1), which was the condition used for cryo-EM structure determination.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions determined empirically.

claim: Single-particle analysis using RELION identified two three-dimensional (3D) classes of particles with distinct conformations in the cytoplasmic domain of Kir6.2.
source: Single-particle analysis using RELION identified two three-dimensional (3D) classes of particles with distinct conformations in the cytoplasmic domain of Kir6.2 (see Discussion below).
evidence: This describes the results of computational analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: The dominant class (~60%) produced a reconstruction with an overall resolution of 6.7 Å (FSC = 0.143) with C4 symmetry imposed.
source: The dominant class (~60%) produced a reconstruction which has an overall resolution of 6.7 Å (FSC = 0.143) with C4 symmetry imposed (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2; Table 1).
evidence: This describes the resolution of the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: With masking, the FSC measurement at 0.143 reached 5.8 Å for the whole channel and 5.1 Å for the Kir6.2 core.
source: With masking the FSC measurement at 0.143 reached 5.8 Å and the Kir6.2 core 5.1 Å.
evidence: This describes the improved resolution with masking.

claim: The other class yielded a reconstruction with an overall unmasked resolution ~7.6 Å.
source: The other class yielded a reconstruction with an overall unmasked resolution ~7.6 Å, and masked whole channel and Kir6.2 core ~7.2 Å and 6.9 Å, respectively.
evidence: This describes the resolution of the second 3D class.

claim: All transmembrane (TM) helices were clearly resolved in the density map (76 total; 17 from each SUR1, 2 from each Kir6.2).
source: All transmembrane (TM) helices were clearly resolved in the density map (76 total; 17 from each SUR1, 2 from each Kir6.2; Figure 2) and contained significant side-chain density which allowed for registration of the models.
evidence: This describes the quality of the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The TM helices contained significant side-chain density which allowed for registration of the models.
source: All transmembrane (TM) helices were clearly resolved in the density map (76 total; 17 from each SUR1, 2 from each Kir6.2; Figure 2) and contained significant side-chain density which allowed for registration of the models.
evidence: This describes the quality of the density map that enabled model building.

claim: The KATP channel is an octamer built around a Kir6.2 tetramer with each subunit complexed to one SUR1.
source: The structure shows that the KATP channel is an octamer built around a Kir6.2 tetramer with each subunit complexed to one SUR1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The KATP complex is ~200 Å in width in the longest dimension and ~125 Å in height.
source: The complex is ~200 Å in width in the longest dimension and ~125 Å in height, and is shaped like a propeller with the Kir6.2 pore and TMD0 forming a compact central core and the SUR1-ABC core structure forming the blades.
evidence: This describes the dimensions measured from the structure.

claim: The KATP complex is shaped like a propeller with the Kir6.2 pore and TMD0 forming a compact central core and the SUR1-ABC core structure forming the blades.
source: The complex is ~200 Å in width in the longest dimension and ~125 Å in height, and is shaped like a propeller with the Kir6.2 pore and TMD0 forming a compact central core and the SUR1-ABC core structure forming the blades.
evidence: This describes the overall architecture observed in the structure.

claim: TMD0 and L0 have been shown to be crucial for channel assembly and gating.
source: A long-standing question has been where TMD0 and L0 are in relation to Kir6.2 and the ABC core structure, as this region has been shown to be crucial for channel assembly and gating (Babenko and Bryan, 2003; Chan et al., 2003; Schwappach et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: An earlier model hypothesized TMD0 to be sandwiched between Kir6.2 and the TMDs of the ABC core.
source: An earlier model hypothesized TMD0 to be sandwiched between Kir6.2 and the TMDs of the ABC core (Bryan et al., 2004), but a later cryo-negative stain single-particle EM study of a channel formed by a SUR1-Kir6.2 fusion protein placed TMD0 next to Kir6.2 in between two adjacent SUR1-ABC core domains (Mikhailov et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes a previous hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: A later cryo-negative stain single-particle EM study placed TMD0 next to Kir6.2 in between two adjacent SUR1-ABC core domains.
source: An earlier model hypothesized TMD0 to be sandwiched between Kir6.2 and the TMDs of the ABC core (Bryan et al., 2004), but a later cryo-negative stain single-particle EM study of a channel formed by a SUR1-Kir6.2 fusion protein placed TMD0 next to Kir6.2 in between two adjacent SUR1-ABC core domains (Mikhailov et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes a previous structural study supported by citation.

claim: In the current structure, TMD0-L0 sits in between the SUR1 and Kir6.2 subunits and is the primary point of contact between the SUR1-ABC core and Kir6.2.
source: In our structure, TMD0-L0 sits in between the SUR1 and Kir6.2 subunits and is the primary point of contact between the SUR1-ABC core and Kir6.2 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the current cryo-EM structure.

claim: The Kir6.2 tetramer is the best resolved region in the complex.
source: The Kir6.2 tetramer is the best resolved region in the complex (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the quality of the density map in different regions.

claim: Side-chain density of many residues in Kir6.2, in particular those in the two TM helices, are visible.
source: Side-chain density of many residues, in particular those in the two TM helices are visible (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the quality of the density map.

claim: The inner helix gate in Kir6.2 is formed by F168 in M2 just below the central cavity.
source: In Kir6.2, the inner helix gate is formed by F168 in M2 just below the central cavity.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: There is only ~6 Å between opposing atoms of the inner helix gate (~3 Å when considering the van der Waals radii).
source: In our model, there is only ~6 Å between opposing atoms of the gate (~3 Å when considering the van der Waals radii), which is too narrow to allow passage of a ~8 Å diameter hydrated K+ ion (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural model.

claim: The inner helix gate is too narrow to allow passage of a ~8 Å diameter hydrated K+ ion.
source: In our model, there is only ~6 Å between opposing atoms of the gate (~3 Å when considering the van der Waals radii), which is too narrow to allow passage of a ~8 Å diameter hydrated K+ ion (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural measurements and known size of hydrated K+ ions.

claim: Comparison of closed and open G-loop structures suggests that the G-loop gate in Kir6.2 is also closed.
source: A comparison of closed (Kir3.2 apostate) and open (Kir3.2-R201A + PIP2) G-loop structures in relation to Kir6.2 suggests that this gate is also closed (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with other Kir channel structures.

claim: The observations indicate a closed channel structure, which is expected since the sample contained saturating concentrations of inhibitory ATP and GBC.
source: Together, these observations indicate a closed channel structure, which is expected since the sample contained saturating concentrations of inhibitory ATP and GBC.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations and experimental conditions.

claim: 3D classification identified two classes with distinct conformations in the cytoplasmic domain (CTD) of Kir6.2 that differ by a rigid-body rotation of the CTD of ~14°.
source: Interestingly, 3D classification identified two classes with distinct conformations in the cytoplasmic domain (CTD) of Kir6.2. The two classes differ by a rigid-body rotation of the CTD of ~14° (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the 3D classification analysis.

claim: A similar rotation has been observed in multiple Kir channel members and has been associated with channel gating.
source: A similar rotation has been observed in multiple Kir channel members and has been associated with channel gating (Clarke et al., 2010; Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: The TMD and gates as well as the density corresponding to bound ATP in both classes are largely unaffected by the CTD rotation.
source: However, the TMD and gates as well as the density corresponding to bound ATP (see below) in both classes are largely unaffected, suggesting rotational freedom for the CTD in the closed state.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two 3D classes.

claim: The CTD rotation suggests rotational freedom for the CTD in the closed state.
source: However, the TMD and gates as well as the density corresponding to bound ATP (see below) in both classes are largely unaffected, suggesting rotational freedom for the CTD in the closed state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Mutagenesis and biochemical studies suggest that ATP binds directly to Kir6.2.
source: Mutagenesis and biochemical studies suggest that ATP binds directly to Kir6.2 (Tanabe et al., 1999; Tucker et al., 1997), and that residues in both N- and C-terminal domains are involved (Antcliff et al., 2005; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Residues in both N- and C-terminal domains of Kir6.2 are involved in ATP binding.
source: Mutagenesis and biochemical studies suggest that ATP binds directly to Kir6.2 (Tanabe et al., 1999; Tucker et al., 1997), and that residues in both N- and C-terminal domains are involved (Antcliff et al., 2005; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Kir6.2 is sensitive to ATP in the absence of SUR1 (IC50 ~100 µM).
source: However, while Kir6.2 is sensitive to ATP in the absence of SUR1 (IC50 ~100 µM), SUR1 increases this sensitivity by ~10-fold (IC50 ~10 µM) (Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: SUR1 increases Kir6.2 ATP sensitivity by ~10-fold (IC50 ~10 µM).
source: However, while Kir6.2 is sensitive to ATP in the absence of SUR1 (IC50 ~100 µM), SUR1 increases this sensitivity by ~10-fold (IC50 ~10 µM) (Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: A prominent bulge in the EM density was observed that is too large to be accounted for by the main chain and the surrounding side-chains.
source: Indeed, we observed a prominent bulge in the EM density that is too large to be accounted for by the main chain and the surrounding side-chains.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The density bulge is about the size of an ATP molecule and is immediately adjacent to K185.
source: The density is about the size of an ATP molecule and is immediately adjacent to K185, a residue that has been implicated in ATP binding (John et al., 2003; Tanabe et al., 1999; Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an observation from the density map combined with knowledge from previous studies.

claim: K185 has been implicated in ATP binding.
source: The density is about the size of an ATP molecule and is immediately adjacent to K185, a residue that has been implicated in ATP binding (John et al., 2003; Tanabe et al., 1999; Tucker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Extensive mutagenesis of K185 has provided strong evidence that this residue is important for binding to the β-phosphate of ATP.
source: Extensive mutagenesis of the K185 residue assessing the effects of various amino acid substitutions on channel sensitivity to inhibition by ATP, ADP, and AMP has provided strong evidence that this residue is important for binding to the β-phosphate of ATP (Jöns et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: The ATP binding pocket is at the interface of adjacent Kir6.2 N and C domains.
source: An overview of the ATP binding site from the side (Figure 4A), and from the top (Figure 4B), with ATP colored in red, illustrates that the pocket is at the interface of adjacent Kir6.2 N and C domains.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The docked ATP is surrounded by residues I182, L205, Y330, F333, and G334 from the same subunit, and R50 from the adjacent subunit.
source: A close-up view (Figure 4C) shows that the docked ATP is surrounded by residues I182, L205, Y330, F333, and G334 from the same subunit, and R50 from the adjacent subunit.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The adenine ring of ATP is pointing toward the N-terminus of subunit A and could be supported by I182, L205, Y330, and F333 of subunit B.
source: The adenine ring is pointing toward the N-terminus of subunit A, and could be supported by I182, L205, Y330, and F333 of subunit B.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: R50 is in a position that would allow it to interact with the γ-phosphate but may also interact with the adenine ring.
source: R50 in subunit A is in a position that would allow it to interact with the γ-phosphate but may also interact with the adenine ring, which would explain mutagenesis data indicating that the interaction of R50 and ATP is not entirely electrostatic (John et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural model and previous mutagenesis data.

claim: K185 is only ~3 Å from the β phosphate of ATP.
source: K185 is only ~3 Å from the β phosphate, while the α-phosphate is close to the main-chain nitrogen of G334 (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural model.

claim: The α-phosphate of ATP is close to the main-chain nitrogen of G334.
source: K185 is only ~3 Å from the β phosphate, while the α-phosphate is close to the main-chain nitrogen of G334 (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: Most residues surrounding the ATP density have been mutated and shown to affect ATP sensitivity.
source: Importantly, most residues surrounding the ATP density have been mutated and shown to affect ATP sensitivity (Antcliff et al., 2005), providing direct validation of our structure.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies that validates the current structure.

claim: The density corresponding to ATP is located on the periphery of the Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain and is traversed by the N-terminal segment of L0 of SUR1 immediately following TMD0.
source: In our structure, we see that the density corresponding to ATP is located on the periphery of the Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain, and traversed by the N-terminal segment of L0 of SUR1 immediately following TMD0 (Figure 4B), with the Cα of K205 coming within only ~10 Å of the site (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The Cα of K205 comes within only ~10 Å of the ATP binding site.
source: In our structure, we see that the density corresponding to ATP is located on the periphery of the Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain, and traversed by the N-terminal segment of L0 of SUR1 immediately following TMD0 (Figure 4B), with the Cα of K205 coming within only ~10 Å of the site (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural model.

claim: Mutation of K205 of L0 to alanine or glutamate reduces ATP sensitivity by ~10-fold.
source: Interestingly, we have previously shown that mutation of K205 of L0 to alanine or glutamate reduce ATP sensitivity by ~10-fold (Pratt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is data from previous work by the authors supported by citation.

claim: The Cα position of K205 lies directly over the ATP binding site and is poised to make electrostatic contribution to ATP binding.
source: While there is no density in the map to allow placement of the K205 side chain, its Cα position lies directly over the site and is poised to make electrostatic contribution to ATP binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural position and chemical properties of K205.

claim: The finding that K205 is positioned near the ATP site offers a mechanism by which SUR1 could enhance the ATP-sensitivity of the Kir6.2 channel.
source: This finding offers a mechanism by which SUR1 could enhance the ATP-sensitivity of the Kir6.2 channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and functional data.

claim: TMD0-L0 is sandwiched between the SUR1-ABC core structure and Kir6.2.
source: As shown in Figure 2, TMD0-L0 is sandwiched between the SUR1-ABC core structure and Kir6.2.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: Densities corresponding to TMD0 and L0 are clearly seen in the map, particularly TMD0, with much of this domain reaching 5 Å resolution.
source: In the map, densities corresponding to TMD0 and L0 are clearly seen, particularly TMD0, with much of this domain reaching 5 Å resolution.
evidence: This describes the quality of the density map in this region.

claim: In a recent cryo-EM study of TAP1/2, TMD0 could not be resolved, possibly because SUR1-TMD0 in the current structure is stabilized by Kir6.2.
source: This is in contrast to a recent cryo-EM study of another ABC transporter containing a TMD0, TAP1/2, where TMD0 could not be resolved (Oldham et al., 2016), possibly because SUR1-TMD0 in our structure is stabilized by Kir6.2.
evidence: This is a comparison with another study and speculation about the reason for better resolution.

claim: TMD0 is a five helix bundle which contains an extracellular N-terminal segment of 25 residues with a brief helical stretch.
source: Overall, TMD0 is a five helix bundle which contains an extracellular N-terminal segment of 25 residues with a brief helical stretch, and mostly short loops connecting helices 2–3, 3–4, and 4–5, but a longer ICL1 of ~14 residues connecting TM1-2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a structural description from the model.

claim: TMD0 has mostly short loops connecting helices 2–3, 3–4, and 4–5, but a longer ICL1 of ~14 residues connecting TM1-2.
source: Overall, TMD0 is a five helix bundle which contains an extracellular N-terminal segment of 25 residues with a brief helical stretch, and mostly short loops connecting helices 2–3, 3–4, and 4–5, but a longer ICL1 of ~14 residues connecting TM1-2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a structural description from the model.

claim: The N-terminus of SUR1 was disordered up until residue C6 where a highly conserved disulfide bond is formed with C26.
source: The N-terminus containing the FLAG-peptide was disordered up until residue C6 of SUR1 where a highly conserved disulfide bond is formed with C26 (Fukuda et al., 2011) at the entrance to TM1.
evidence: This is a structural observation combined with knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The N-terminal region of TMD0 contacts the Kir6.2 turret and pore loop.
source: This region contacts the Kir6.2 turret and pore loop (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a role in assembly and functional coupling with the pore.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The N-terminal region of TMD0 has a role in assembly and functional coupling with the pore.
source: This region contacts the Kir6.2 turret and pore loop (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a role in assembly and functional coupling with the pore.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: A number of HI-causing mutations in the N-terminal extracellular loop of TMD0 including C6G, G7R, V21D, N24K, and C26S disrupt channel biogenesis efficiency or gating.
source: A number of HI-causing mutations in the N-terminal extracellular loop of TMD0 including C6G, G7R, V21D, N24K, and C26S, which disrupt channel biogenesis efficiency or gating have been reported (Martin et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2007), further supporting the significance of this region in channel assembly and gating.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: TM1 of TMD0 and the M1 helix of Kir6.2 are the primary sites of interaction in the transmembrane region.
source: In the transmembrane region, TM1 of TMD0 and the M1 helix of Kir6.2 are the primary sites of interaction.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: TM1 and M1 helices make close contact throughout their entire length.
source: These helices make close contact throughout their entire length (Figure 5A) and at residue P45 in TM1, a kink is introduced that places the trajectory of the two helices in alignment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: At residue P45 in TM1, a kink is introduced that places the trajectory of the two helices in alignment.
source: These helices make close contact throughout their entire length (Figure 5A) and at residue P45 in TM1, a kink is introduced that places the trajectory of the two helices in alignment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: There are many potential hydrophobic interactions between opposing faces of TM1 and M1 helices, which may facilitate association of the complex.
source: There are many potential hydrophobic interactions between opposing faces of these helices, which may facilitate association of the complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Multiple HI-causing mutations in TM1 of TMD0 (F27S, A30T, L31P, L40R) have been shown to impair channel assembly and surface expression.
source: Indeed, multiple HI-causing mutations in TM1 of TMD0 (F27S, A30T, L31P, L40R) have been shown to impair channel assembly and surface expression (Martin et al., 2016), likely by disrupting interactions between the two helices.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: HI-causing mutations in TM1 likely impair channel assembly by disrupting interactions between TM1 and M1 helices.
source: Indeed, multiple HI-causing mutations in TM1 of TMD0 (F27S, A30T, L31P, L40R) have been shown to impair channel assembly and surface expression (Martin et al., 2016), likely by disrupting interactions between the two helices.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and functional data.

claim: There are intimate interactions between the ICLs of TMD0, the start of L0, the Kir6.2 PIP2 binding pocket, and the Kir6.2 ATP binding pocket on the cytoplasmic side.
source: On the cytoplasmic side, there are intimate interactions between the ICLs of TMD0, the start of L0, the Kir6.2 PIP2 binding pocket (cytoplasmic ends of M1 and M2 helices) identified based on other PIP2-bound Kir structures (Hansen et al., 2011; Whorton and MacKinnon, 2011), and the Kir6.2 ATP binding pocket.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The hypothetically docked PIP2 is surrounded by ICL2 (E128-P133) of TMD0, the N-terminal stretch of L0 (K192-K199) from one SUR1 subunit, and the cytoplasmic end of TM1 (K57) of TMD0 from the adjacent SUR1 subunit.
source: As shown in Figure 5B and C, the hypothetically docked PIP2 is surrounded by the cytoplasmic loop connecting TM3 and 4 (ICL2; E128-P133) of TMD0 and the N-terminal stretch of L0 (K192-K199) from one SUR1 subunit, and the cytoplasmic end of TM1 (K57) of TMD0 from the adjacent SUR1 subunit.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model with hypothetically docked PIP2.

claim: Previous studies have shown that TMD0 and the N-terminal section of L0 increase the Po of Kir6.2 to resemble intact channels.
source: Previous studies have shown that TMD0 and the N-terminal section of L0 increase the Po of Kir6.2 to resemble intact channels (Babenko and Bryan, 2003; Chan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: TMD0 and L0 regions may contribute directly to PIP2 binding to account for the increase in PIP2 sensitivity conferred by SUR1.
source: As Po is determined by PIP2 interactions, our structure suggests these regions may contribute directly to PIP2 binding to account for the increase in PIP2 sensitivity conferred by SUR1 (Enkvetchakul et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and previous functional data.

claim: ATP is located below PIP2 and is separated from PIP2 by L0 and ICL2 of TMD0.
source: Below PIP2 and near the periphery of Kir6.2 lies ATP, separated from PIP2 by L0 (Figure 5B,C) and also ICL2 of TMD0 (Figure 5B,E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: ICL2 sits directly atop the Kir6.2 N-terminus, just before the interfacial helix at Q52.
source: The ICL2 sits directly atop the Kir6.2 N-terminus, just before the interfacial helix (i.e. the 'slide helix') at Q52 (Figure 5D), and simultaneously contacts ICL1 of TMD0 and the most C-terminal portion of TMD0 at TM5.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: ICL2 simultaneously contacts ICL1 of TMD0 and the most C-terminal portion of TMD0 at TM5.
source: The ICL2 sits directly atop the Kir6.2 N-terminus, just before the interfacial helix (i.e. the 'slide helix') at Q52 (Figure 5D), and simultaneously contacts ICL1 of TMD0 and the most C-terminal portion of TMD0 at TM5.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: Mutation of E128 (E128K, a HI mutation) and F132 (F132L, a PNDM mutation) in ICL2 as well as Q52 in Kir6.2 (Q52R, a PNDM mutation) disrupts channel gating by ATP and PIP2.
source: Mutation of E128 (E128K, a HI mutation) and F132 (F132L, a PNDM mutation) in ICL2 as well as Q52 in Kir6.2 (Q52R, a PNDM mutation) is known to disrupt channel gating by ATP and PIP2 (Pratt et al., 2009; Proks et al., 2004, 2006) (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: The ICL2 region is well positioned to contribute to gating regulation by both ATP and PIP2, explaining the effects of disease mutations.
source: Our finding that this region is close to both the ATP and PIP2 sites illustrates that it is well positioned to contribute to gating regulation by both, explaining the effects of these disease mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and functional data.

claim: L0 is nestled between TMD0 and the ABC core of SUR1 and comprises ~90 amino acids.
source: L0 (i.e. ICL3) is nestled between TMD0 and the ABC core of SUR1, and comprises ~90 amino acids.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: L0 was modeled as a polyalanine chain with two helical segments, one from L224-A240 and the other from L260-D277.
source: We have modeled L0 as a polyalanine chain with two helical segments that are strongly supported by the map, one an amphipathic helix from L224-A240 and the other from L260-D277, which connects to TMD1.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach and structural features observed.

claim: The N- and C-terminal stretches of L0 make a 'V,' with the intervening sequence (L213-L260) forming a hairpin structure at the apex.
source: In the model, the N- and C-terminal stretches of L0 make a 'V,' with the intervening sequence (L213-L260) forming a hairpin structure at the apex (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a structural description from the model.

claim: The hairpin structure of L0 is simultaneously bridging multiple sites within TMD0 with the ABC core structure (TMs 15 + 16), and may also interact with the Kir6.2 N-terminus (A45-Q52).
source: This hairpin structure is simultaneously bridging multiple sites within TMD0 with the ABC core structure (TMs 15 + 16), and may also interact with the Kir6.2 N-terminus (A45-Q52), which would allow L0 to transduce signals from the ABC core to gate the channel.
evidence: This is a structural observation and inference about functional implications.

claim: L0 could transduce signals from the ABC core to gate the channel.
source: This hairpin structure is simultaneously bridging multiple sites within TMD0 with the ABC core structure (TMs 15 + 16), and may also interact with the Kir6.2 N-terminus (A45-Q52), which would allow L0 to transduce signals from the ABC core to gate the channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The strategic placement of L0 is consistent with its multiple functional roles including regulation of channel Po, sensitivity to ATP inhibition, and sensitivity to Mg-nucleotide stimulation.
source: The strategic placement of L0 is consistent with its multiple functional roles reported, including regulation of channel Po, sensitivity to ATP inhibition, and sensitivity to Mg-nucleotide stimulation (Babenko and Bryan, 2003; Chan et al., 2003; Masia et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and previous functional studies.

claim: L0 has been reported to interact with GBC.
source: Another role of L0 that has been reported is interaction with GBC (Winkler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: GBC is a second-generation sulfonylurea containing a sulfonylurea group and a benzamido moiety that binds KATP channels with nanomolar affinity (KD ~1 nM).
source: GBC is a second-generation sulfonylurea containing a sulfonylurea group and a benzamido moiety that binds KATP channels with nanomolar affinity (KD ~1 nM) (Gribble and Reimann, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: L0 has been proposed to participate in binding to the benzamido group of GBC, with mutation Y230A in L0 reducing GBC binding.
source: L0 has been proposed to participate in binding to the benzamido group, with mutation Y230A in L0 reducing GBC binding.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The amphipathic helix of L0 containing Y230 sits next to TM16 containing S1238.
source: We find that the amphipathic helix of L0 containing Y230 sits next to TM16 containing S1238, a residue which when mutated disrupts binding of the sulfonylurea group (Ashfield et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: Mutation of S1238 disrupts binding of the sulfonylurea group.
source: We find that the amphipathic helix of L0 containing Y230 sits next to TM16 containing S1238, a residue which when mutated disrupts binding of the sulfonylurea group (Ashfield et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: Y230 and S1238 are separated by ~20 Å (Cα to Cα), which explains how the two residues distant in the primary sequence can both contribute to GBC binding.
source: The two residues are separated by ~20 Å (Cα to Cα), which explains how the two residues distant in the primary sequence can both contribute to binding.
evidence: This is a measurement from the model and an inference about functional implications.

claim: At the current resolution, the density for GBC cannot be discerned, but it is likely to be bound given its high affinity.
source: Although at the current resolution, we are unable to discern the density for GBC, it is likely to be bound given its high affinity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental conditions and known binding affinity.

claim: The SUR1 core is built from two homologous halves, TMD1-NBD1 and TMD2-NBD2.
source: The SUR1 core is built from two homologous halves, TMD1-NBD1 and TMD2-NBD2.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: Each of the 12 combined TM helices from both TMD1 and TMD2 are clearly resolved, as well as the short lateral 'elbow' helices leading into the first helix of each TMD (TM6 and TM12).
source: Each of the 12 combined TM helices from both TMD1 and TMD2 are clearly resolved, as well as the short lateral 'elbow' helices leading into the first helix of each TMD (TM6 and TM12) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This describes the quality of the density map.

claim: There is a domain swap at the extracellular linker between helices 3 and 4 of each TMD, characteristic of other ABC exporters.
source: Characteristic of other ABC exporters, there is a domain swap at the extracellular linker between helices 3 and 4 of each TMD (Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2015), such that each 'half' of the ABC core is composed of TMs 1–3, and 6 of one TMD, plus TMs 4 and 5 of the other (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a structural observation consistent with other ABC exporters, supported by citations.

claim: Each 'half' of the ABC core is composed of TMs 1–3, and 6 of one TMD, plus TMs 4 and 5 of the other.
source: Characteristic of other ABC exporters, there is a domain swap at the extracellular linker between helices 3 and 4 of each TMD (Jin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2015), such that each 'half' of the ABC core is composed of TMs 1–3, and 6 of one TMD, plus TMs 4 and 5 of the other (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The SUR1-ABC core is in an inward-facing conformation with the NBDs clearly separated.
source: Overall, the SUR1-ABC core is in an inward-facing conformation, with the NBDs clearly separated (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The inward-facing conformation is consistent with other ABC exporter structures solved without Mg-nucleotides.
source: This is consistent with other ABC exporter structures solved without Mg-nucleotides.
evidence: This is a comparison with other known structures.

claim: In other ABC exporters, transporter halves are related by either a true or a pseudo two-fold symmetry axis.
source: However, in contrast to other ABC exporters of known structure whereby transporter halves are related by either a true or a pseudo two-fold symmetry axis, depending on whether the two halves are identical or not (Wilkens, 2015), we find a clear rotation and a translation of TMD1-NBD1 relative to TMD2-NDB2, such that TMD1-NBD1 is ~15° off the symmetry axis and is translated by ~10 Å horizontally (relative to the membrane) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about other ABC exporters supported by citation.

claim: In the SUR1 structure, there is a clear rotation and a translation of TMD1-NBD1 relative to TMD2-NDB2, such that TMD1-NBD1 is ~15° off the symmetry axis and is translated by ~10 Å horizontally.
source: However, in contrast to other ABC exporters of known structure whereby transporter halves are related by either a true or a pseudo two-fold symmetry axis, depending on whether the two halves are identical or not (Wilkens, 2015), we find a clear rotation and a translation of TMD1-NBD1 relative to TMD2-NDB2, such that TMD1-NBD1 is ~15° off the symmetry axis and is translated by ~10 Å horizontally (relative to the membrane) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: In the observed configuration, the SUR1 NBDs likely could not dimerize without a twisting motion to align the dimerization interface.
source: In this configuration, the SUR1 NBDs likely could not dimerize without a twisting motion to align the dimerization interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: Dimerization of NBDs in SUR1 has been proposed to follow MgATP hydrolysis or MgADP binding to stimulate channel activity.
source: Dimerization of NBDs in SUR1 has been proposed to follow MgATP hydrolysis or MgADP binding to stimulate channel activity (Nichols, 2006), and GBC inhibits channel activity by preventing Mg-nucleotide stimulation (de Wet and Proks, 2015; Gribble and Reimann, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: GBC inhibits channel activity by preventing Mg-nucleotide stimulation.
source: Dimerization of NBDs in SUR1 has been proposed to follow MgATP hydrolysis or MgADP binding to stimulate channel activity (Nichols, 2006), and GBC inhibits channel activity by preventing Mg-nucleotide stimulation (de Wet and Proks, 2015; Gribble and Reimann, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: The twisted conformation may be caused by GBC binding, which would suggest that GBC prevents MgADP from stimulating the channel by causing a misalignment of the NBDs dimerization interface.
source: As discussed above, given its high-affinity GBC is likely to be bound in our structure. Thus, an interesting hypothesis is that the twisted conformation is caused by GBC binding, which would suggest that GBC prevents MgADP from stimulating the channel by causing a misalignment of the NBDs dimerization interface.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observation and known properties of GBC.

claim: Alternatively, the twisted conformation may be unique to SUR1 and Mg-nucleotide binding/hydrolysis may be required to restore symmetry for dimerization.
source: Alternatively, the conformation may be unique to SUR1 and that Mg-nucleotide binding/hydrolysis is required to restore symmetry for dimerization.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis.

claim: GBC may block stimulation by clamping down L0 and preventing it from communicating with Kir6.2.
source: In this case, GBC may block stimulation by clamping down L0 and preventing it from communicating with Kir6.2.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism.

claim: The ABC core of SUR1 switches between an inward-facing and outward-facing conformations as MgATP undergoes hydrolysis or as MgADP binds at NBD2 and induces NBD dimerization.
source: We propose that like other ABC transporters (Wilkens, 2015), the ABC core of SUR1 switches between an inward-facing and outward-facing conformations as MgATP undergoes hydrolysis or as MgADP binds at NBD2 and induces NBD dimerization.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structure and knowledge of other ABC transporters.

claim: The conformational switch at the ABC core causes movement of the L0 and TMD0, which alters channel interactions with ATP and PIP2 by remodeling the interface.
source: The conformational switch at the ABC core causes movement of the L0 and TMD0, which alters channel interactions with ATP and PIP2 by remodeling the interface formed by the cytoplasmic domain of Kir6.2, the bottom of the Kir6.2 transmembrane helices, the intracellular loops of TMD0 and the N-terminal segment of L0.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The SUR1 'transport' cycle is coupled to Kir6.2 opening or closing rather than transport of substrates through SUR1 itself.
source: In this way, the SUR1 'transport' cycle is coupled to Kir6.2 opening or closing rather than transport of substrates through SUR1 itself.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The structure highlights the critical role of SUR1-TMD0 in the association of the two subunits.
source: Our structure highlights the critical role of SUR1-TMD0 in the association of the two subunits.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural observations.

claim: TMD0 appears to harbor more mutations that disrupt channel biogenesis and trafficking than other regions of SUR1.
source: Indeed, TMD0 appears to harbor more mutations that disrupt channel biogenesis and trafficking than other regions of SUR1 (Martin et al., 2013, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Many mutations in TMD0 which impair channel biogenesis and trafficking can be rescued by pharmacological chaperones, specifically sulfonylureas such as GBC.
source: It is worth noting that many mutations in TMD0 which impair channel biogenesis and trafficking can be rescued by pharmacological chaperones, specifically sulfonylureas such as GBC (Chen et al., 2013a; Martin et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2004, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: GBC may alter structural interactions between TMD0 and Kir6.2 to correct biogenesis/trafficking defects caused by TMD0 mutations.
source: As our structure is obtained in the presence of GBC, an important question to address in the future is whether GBC alters structural interactions between TMD0 and Kir6.2 to correct biogenesis/trafficking defects caused by TMD0 mutations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis for future investigation.

claim: Part of L0 (from a.a. 214 on) is conserved in CFTR and the multidrug resistance-associated proteins MRPs.
source: Part of L0 (from a.a. 214 on) is conserved in CFTR and the multidrug resistance-associated proteins MRPs (Zhang and Chen, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the CFTR structure, the loop corresponding to L0 contains an amphipathic helix followed by another helix before the elbow helix.
source: Interestingly, in the recently reported CFTR structure, this loop which the authors named the 'lasso motif' also contains an amphipathic helix followed by another helix before the elbow helix (Zhang and Chen, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a recent study supported by citation.

claim: The structural model of L0 is in line with the CFTR model of the corresponding loop.
source: Our structural model of L0 is in line with the CFTR model of the corresponding loop.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current structure and the CFTR structure.

claim: In CFTR, the loop corresponding to L0 has been shown to be involved in trafficking regulation by syntaxin 1A.
source: In CFTR or MRP-1, this loop has been shown to be involved in trafficking regulation by syntaxin 1A (Naren et al., 1998; Peters et al., 2001) or association with the plasma membrane (Bakos et al., 2000), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: In MRP-1, the loop corresponding to L0 has been shown to be involved in association with the plasma membrane.
source: In CFTR or MRP-1, this loop has been shown to be involved in trafficking regulation by syntaxin 1A (Naren et al., 1998; Peters et al., 2001) or association with the plasma membrane (Bakos et al., 2000), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Close examination of the zebrafish CFTR structure where the inhibitory R-domain is present indicates misalignment of the two NBDs.
source: Intriguingly, close examination of the recently published zebrafish CFTR structure where the inhibitory R-domain is present (Zhang and Chen, 2016) and the TAP transporter structure with an inhibitory viral peptide bound (Oldham et al., 2016) also indicates misalignment of the two NBDs albeit to lesser degrees, further suggesting that NBDs misalignment may be a common theme in ABC transporters bound to inhibitory ligands.
evidence: This is an observation from examining other published structures.

claim: The TAP transporter structure with an inhibitory viral peptide bound indicates misalignment of the two NBDs.
source: Intriguingly, close examination of the recently published zebrafish CFTR structure where the inhibitory R-domain is present (Zhang and Chen, 2016) and the TAP transporter structure with an inhibitory viral peptide bound (Oldham et al., 2016) also indicates misalignment of the two NBDs albeit to lesser degrees, further suggesting that NBDs misalignment may be a common theme in ABC transporters bound to inhibitory ligands.
evidence: This is an observation from examining other published structures.

claim: NBDs misalignment may be a common theme in ABC transporters bound to inhibitory ligands.
source: Intriguingly, close examination of the recently published zebrafish CFTR structure where the inhibitory R-domain is present (Zhang and Chen, 2016) and the TAP transporter structure with an inhibitory viral peptide bound (Oldham et al., 2016) also indicates misalignment of the two NBDs albeit to lesser degrees, further suggesting that NBDs misalignment may be a common theme in ABC transporters bound to inhibitory ligands.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations from multiple structures.

claim: Some regions known to be important for channel assembly and gating such as the distal N- and C-termini of Kir6.2 as well as several linker loops in SUR1 are not well resolved in the current map.
source: Some regions known to be important for channel assembly and gating such as the distal N- and C-termini of Kir6.2 as well as several linker loops in SUR1 are not well resolved in the current map (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes limitations of the current structure.
